title: Fourth commandment (CCC 2197–2257)
hookLine: honor parents, and parents and leaders serve those in their care

cards: A plastic pill organizer, seven little doors, morning and night. On a weeknight, a woman in her forties fills it for her father. He watches from the doorway, a little embarrassed, a little grateful.
Forty years ago, he was the one cutting her grapes in half so she wouldn't choke. Neither of them says anything about it. The roles have quietly turned over.
The fourth commandment lives right there, in the turning.

teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "Honour thy father and thy mother." The Catechism says this commandment opens the second part of the law, the part about neighbors, and it starts at home, in the family it calls a domestic church.
For children, honor means respect, gratitude and, while they live at home, obedience.

teach.h: GROWN CHILDREN: CARE IN OLD AGE.
teach.b: And it doesn't expire: grown children owe their parents help in old age, sickness, loneliness and distress, as far as they can.
The book of Sirach, which the Catechism quotes, asks a son to help his father in his old age and not to grieve him, even if his mind fails. Then the commandment turns around.
Parents have duties too: to see their children as children of God, to educate them, to be the first to hand on the faith, and to respect their freedom, including their calling in life.
Paul writes in Ephesians: fathers, "provoke not your children to anger."
And the circle widens to anyone with authority, which the Catechism says must be used as a service; Jesus tells his followers that whoever would be great among them must be their servant.
Even Jesus, found in the temple at twelve, goes home to Nazareth with Mary and Joseph, and Luke says he "was subject to them." Honor flows up and down at once.
The week in one breath: written in reason, his gift in us, the minimum not the maximum, God first, names are holy, keep holy the day, and now this.

how: Catholics are taught to honor and care for their parents throughout life; parents promise at a child's baptism to raise them in the faith, and the Church calls the family a domestic church.

games.q: you're twelve. after three days of searching, your worried parents find you in the temple among the teachers. you've told them you must be about your Father's business. what next?
o: stay in the temple; your work matters more.
go home to Nazareth with them, and be subject to them.
send them home and follow later.
games.why: in Luke 2, Jesus goes down with Mary and Joseph to Nazareth and was subject to them.

practice: Bring to mind a parent, a grandparent or an older person who looked after you, even imperfectly, and let one specific thing they did come back: a meal, a ride, a hard word that turned out right.
If they're living, find the words you'd use to thank them; if they've died, thank them in silence; if the relationship is painful, choose another elder instead. If you pray, ask God to bless them.

wordCard.voice: Fourth commandment. Honor your father and mother: children honor and care for parents, and parents, and all in authority, serve those in their care. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: honor flows both ways. Children honor, and those in authority serve. That's the week.
